title: Sales Call Scorecard
subtitle: Eight dimensions for the caller, eight factors for the lead, applied to every recorded sales call.
offerContextPlaceholder: [OFFER CONTEXT — replace this paragraph during setup. Describe what the business sells, to whom, at what price points, and what language the pitch should use. The scorer uses this to judge whether a pitch was on-message. See the setup manual.]
scoringPrinciples: No weighting. Every dimension counts equally, because a weakness in any single one can kill the deal.
Every judgement must be anchored to a specific moment in the transcript. Quote the exact words so they can find the moment.

Every quote carries the time it happened, written as [mm:ss] immediately after the closing quotation mark — "I have nothing to show for it" [03:50]. Take the time from the transcript's own timestamps; never estimate one. If a line in the transcript carries no timestamp, quote it without one rather than inventing a number.

You are scoring two separate things and must not let one bleed into the other: the caller's execution, and the quality of the lead they were handed. A weak lead does not lower the caller's scores, and a strong lead does not raise them.
Be direct. If the call was bad, say so. If a dimension scored a 3, explain exactly why without softening it.
Do not over-praise. A 7 is a good score. An 8 is strong. A 9 means near-flawless execution on that dimension. A 10 is reserved for exceptional, textbook-worthy moments.

If the transcript gives no evidence for a dimension — it never came up, or the call ended before it could — return 0 for that score and say in the reasoning what was missing. 0 means not assessed, never a score of zero out of ten; it is left blank on the tracker and drops out of every average. Never fill the gap with a middle score; a guessed number poisons every average built on it.

dimensions.name: Frame Ownership
dimensions.plainQuestion: Who was steering — the caller or the prospect?
dimensions.question: Did the caller control the conversation's direction, pacing, and agenda throughout?
dimensions.detail: Did they set the frame at the top using a structured opening that establishes discovery first, then solution, then decision? When the prospect tried to derail — asking about pricing early, skipping discovery, going on tangents — did the caller redirect smoothly? The person who controls the frame controls the outcome.

bands.text: Prospect led the conversation. Caller was reactive, answered questions out of sequence, let the prospect skip discovery.
Frame was set at the start but lost at some point and not recovered. Prospect dictated pace for portions of the call.
Frame held throughout with natural redirects. Caller transitioned between phases deliberately.
The prospect never questioned who was leading. Caller moved through discovery, pitch and close with total control.

flags: Did the caller use a structured frame-setting opener?
Did the caller give the prospect the illusion of control ("Where do you think we should go from here?")?
Did the caller allow the prospect to interview them instead of the other way around?

dimensions.name: Discovery Depth
dimensions.plainQuestion: Did they get past the first answer to the real problem?
dimensions.question: How many layers deep did the caller go?
dimensions.detail: Surface-level discovery ("What's your biggest challenge?" then moving on) is a 3 at best. The standard is getting past the business problem into the personal impact, quantifying the gap with real numbers, and making the prospect articulate what happens if nothing changes. The test: by the end of discovery, could you write a one-paragraph summary of the prospect's exact situation, the emotional weight behind it, and why now matters, using only what they told the caller? If yes, that is an 8 or above.

bands.text: Surface-level answers accepted without probing. Caller moved to pitch without understanding the real situation.
Got to the business problem but not the personal or emotional layer. Some numbers gathered but gaps remain.
Full excavation — business metrics, personal impact, financial specifics, timeline, emotional drivers. The gap between current and desired situation is crystal clear.
The prospect had a visible emotional moment or said something like "I've never actually told anyone that." Discovery created genuine self-awareness in the prospect.

flags: Did the caller quantify the problem in numbers (revenue, profit, overhead, client count, hours worked)?
Did the caller chunk down into specifics rather than accepting the first answer?
Did the caller ask how long the problem has been going on?
Did the caller connect the business problem to personal or life impact?
Did the caller ask what happens if nothing changes in six months?
Did the caller assess what the prospect has already tried and why it did not work?

dimensions.name: Belief Architecture
dimensions.plainQuestion: Did they make the prospect want it before pitching it?
dimensions.question: Were the seven buying beliefs built during the call?
dimensions.detail: There are seven beliefs a prospect must hold before they will buy: Pain (they have a real gap), Doubt (they cannot fix it alone), Cost (inaction is more expensive than action), Desire (solving this leads to a better future), Money (they can and should invest), Support (the people around them back the decision), Trust (this specific method is the right one). Score this as an integrated structure, not a checklist. Every objection at the close that was not pre-handled is evidence of a failure here.

bands.text: Multiple beliefs unaddressed. Objections at the close caught the caller off guard.
Covered most beliefs but missed at least one that later surfaced as an objection.
All relevant beliefs addressed during discovery. The only objections at the close were purely financial or logistical.
Zero uncertainty objections. The close was about logistics only.

flags: Did the caller introduce doubt ("What's been stopping you from figuring this out by yourself?")?
Did the caller establish the cost of inaction?
Did the caller check for partner or decision-maker support early?
Did the caller uncover past solutions and position against them?
Did the caller paint the desired future vividly enough to create urgency?
Name the specific beliefs that were weakest or missing.

dimensions.name: Pitch Precision
dimensions.plainQuestion: Was the pitch built for this prospect, or could it have been for anyone?
dimensions.question: Was the pitch custom-built for this prospect, and did it sell the transformation rather than the deliverables?
dimensions.detail: Two things matter. First, did the pitch reference specific things the prospect said in discovery — their exact words, their numbers, their personal goals — or could it have been delivered to anyone? Second, did the caller pitch the transformation or the deliverables? Describing what you will do is weak. Describing what changes for the prospect as a result is strong. The strong shape is a bridge built from discovery: name the deliverable, connect it to the logical benefit, then to the emotional benefit, and tie down after each pillar — or open with the prospect's own words: "You told me [their pain]... so what we do is [solution]... so that you can [what changes for them]." A pitch assembled this way cannot be generic.

bands.text: Generic pitch. Mostly deliverables. Could have been said to anyone on any call.
Referenced some discovery details but still leaned on deliverables and features.
Fully tailored, transformation-led, tied down after each pillar.
The prospect interrupted to say "that's exactly what I need" before the caller finished.

flags: Did the caller use the prospect's own words in the pitch?
Did the caller tie the solution to the prospect's specific desired outcome rather than a generic one?
Did the caller tie down after each pillar ("Make sense?" / "What questions do you have on that?")?
Did the caller pitch deliverables instead of transformation?
Was the delivery section kept simple, or did it overwhelm the prospect?

dimensions.name: Tension Management
dimensions.plainQuestion: Could they sit in silence after saying the price?
dimensions.question: Could the caller hold tension without becoming needy?
dimensions.detail: This is the difference between people who have great conversations and people who close. Can the caller hold silence after dropping the price? Ask uncomfortable questions about finances without flinching? Push back on "I need to think about it" without sounding desperate? Any sign of neediness tanks this score: rushed or urgent tone, getting excited when the prospect agrees to pay, accepting a counter-offer too quickly, overpromising to win the sale, filling silence after the price drop, or softening the price.

bands.text: Broke tension consistently — filled silences, softened the price, backed off objections quickly.
Handled some tense moments well but folded on at least one key moment.
Held tension throughout. Comfortable with silence and hard questions. Never sounded needy.
Used tension strategically to create movement — not just endured it but leveraged it.

flags: What happened immediately after the price drop? The correct answer is nothing — the caller stops talking.
Did the caller ever sound like they needed the sale?
Did the caller ask hard financial questions directly?
Did the caller back down from a push too early?

dimensions.name: Objection Resolution
dimensions.plainQuestion: Did they find the real objection before answering it?
dimensions.question: Were objections handled in the correct sequence?
dimensions.detail: The sequence is: drop the investment and stop talking, pace the first objection without reacting, tie down certainty ("Finances aside, do you feel like this is what you need?"), handle any uncertainty objections first, and only then handle financial or partner objections. The biggest error is treating a certainty problem as a money problem. If the prospect is not sold and the caller jumps into payment plans, that is a critical failure.

bands.text: Reacted to surface objections. Did not isolate the real objection. Jumped to payment plans before confirming certainty.
Paced and isolated but handled in the wrong order, or missed the real objection behind a surface one.
Clean sequence — paced, isolated, handled uncertainty before money, referenced discovery throughout.
Turned the objection into a reason to buy.

flags: Did the caller pace the first objection rather than rebutting it?
Did the caller isolate the real objection?
Did the caller use consistency ("You told me earlier that...")?
Did the caller handle uncertainty before money?
Was the tonality neutral and grounded, or harsh, quick and defensive?

dimensions.name: Qualification
dimensions.plainQuestion: Did they check this was a real buyer, and act on what they found?
dimensions.question: Did the caller establish early whether this is a real prospect, and act on what they found?
dimensions.detail: Key areas: can this person decide alone or is there a partner, do they have financial capacity, is the timing right, are they shopping around. This is also about acting on what you find. Identifying that a business partner exists and then ignoring it until it surfaces as an objection at the close is a failure. Disqualifying too early and missing a real opportunity is the opposite failure.

bands.text: No qualification. Pitched everyone the same regardless of signals.
Some qualification but did not act on red flags or adjust the approach.
Qualified decisively — decision-makers identified, financial capacity checked, timing confirmed, approach adjusted accordingly.
The entire call strategy was shaped by qualification findings. Nothing at the close was a surprise.

flags: Did the caller check for decision-maker status (partner, spouse, board)?
Did the caller financially pre-qualify before going deep?
Did the caller recognise an uncloseable prospect and handle it efficiently?
If a two-call close was appropriate, did the caller set it up correctly?
Did the caller book a follow-up when they should have pushed harder? Follow-ups close at under 10 percent, so this is almost always a mistake.

dimensions.name: Strategic Awareness
dimensions.plainQuestion: Did they notice what was happening on the call and adjust?
dimensions.question: Did the caller read the room and adapt in real time?
dimensions.detail: The meta-dimension. Were there moments the caller clearly missed? Did they misread the prospect's certainty level? Did they stay too long in discovery when the prospect was ready to move, or rush the pitch when more discovery was needed? This is about pattern recognition and real-time adaptation.

bands.text: Major misreads. Moved to pitch when the prospect was not ready, or spent forty minutes in discovery when the prospect was already sold. Missed obvious buying signals or red flags.
Read the room mostly right but missed secondary signals. Some mismatch between prospect energy and the caller's approach.
Accurate reads throughout. Adapted pace and approach to the prospect's energy. Knew when to push and when to back off.
Identified and exploited the exact moment the prospect was ready to move. Perfect pacing. Every transition felt natural and well-timed.

flags: Were there buying signals that went unnoticed?
Were there red flags that got ignored?
Did the caller spend too long or too little on any phase?
Was there a moment where a different move would have changed the outcome?

leadQuality.intro: The eight dimensions above score the caller. This section scores the lead they were handed. It exists so a bad number can be traced to the right cause: a closer who executed badly, or a prospect who was never going to buy. Score only what the prospect said and did, never what the caller asserted on their behalf. Where a subject came up and the answer was vague, score the band the evidence supports. Where it never came up at all — the caller did not ask and the prospect did not volunteer — return 0 and say what was missing. 0 means not assessed, never a score of zero; it is left blank on the tracker and drops out of the Lead Score. A guessed middle score here is worse than no score, because it makes an unknown lead look like an average one.

factors.name: Pain Severity
factors.question: How badly is the prospect's current situation actually hurting them?
factors.detail: Score the pain the prospect described, not the pain the caller asserted on their behalf. Three things raise it: how long it has gone on, whether it is quantified in real numbers, and whether it reaches past the business into their life, health, relationships or self-image. A prospect who is mildly dissatisfied buys nothing regardless of who is on the call.

bands.text: Mild dissatisfaction, or pain the caller described for them. No duration, no numbers, no personal cost.
Real and sustained problem, stated in their own words, but contained to the business and not quantified.
Quantified, long-running and personal. They named what it costs them and it reached beyond work.

factors.name: Urgency
factors.question: Is there a reason this has to be solved now rather than in six months?
factors.detail: Separate internal urgency — frustration, a self-imposed deadline, being fed up — from an external forcing function, such as a contract ending, a funded account expiring, a season closing, or money running out on a date they named. External beats internal every time. General frustration with no deadline is the most common false positive in this whole rubric: it feels urgent on the call and defers the moment the call ends.

bands.text: No urgency. Exploring, curious, or 'sometime this year'. Nothing changes if they do nothing.
Internal urgency only — real frustration and a wish to move faster, but no date and nothing forcing it.
An external forcing function with a date attached, or a cost of waiting the prospect themselves quantified.

factors.name: Desire Clarity
factors.question: Can the prospect describe the specific outcome they want?
factors.detail: "I want to be profitable" is vague. "Five thousand a month by March so I can hand in my notice" is clear. Score the specificity of the destination — a number, a date, a named change in their life — and whether an emotional anchor is attached to it. A prospect who cannot name the outcome cannot recognise it when it is sold to them.

bands.text: No stated outcome, or a direction so general it could belong to anyone.
Clear direction and a real motivation, but no number, no date, or no concrete picture of the destination.
A specific outcome with a figure or a deadline, tied to something that matters to them personally.

factors.name: Solution Belief
factors.question: Does the prospect believe this kind of solution works?
factors.detail: Belief in the category and the method — mentorship, coaching, the approach being sold — not yet belief in this particular provider. A prospect who arrived already sold on the concept and is only choosing between providers scores high. Active scepticism about the whole category, or a belief that everyone selling it is a scammer, scores low.

bands.text: Sceptical of the category. Treats the approach, or the people selling it, as unproven or dishonest.
Open to it without conviction. Willing to hear the case but has not decided the approach is the answer.
Pre-sold on the method. Sought it out, named it themselves, or referenced others it worked for.

factors.name: Self-Efficacy
factors.question: Does the prospect believe they can execute it, while accepting they need help to do so?
factors.detail: This factor is not monotonic, and scoring it as 'more is better' gets it backwards. Some doubt is required to buy: a prospect certain they can fix it alone has no reason to pay anyone. But a prospect who does not believe they could succeed even with help will not commit either — they defer, because committing risks proving something about themselves. The buyable zone is the middle: they accept they need outside help and still believe they can do the work. Score how favourable the position is for a close, not how much confidence is present.

bands.text: Either extreme. Certain they can do it alone and just gathering information, or visibly doubting they can succeed at all.
Leaning to one end. Mostly self-reliant, or carrying self-doubt that is likely to surface as hesitation at the close.
The buyable zone. Openly needs help, still believes they can execute once they have it.

factors.name: Authority
factors.question: Can this person decide alone, and do the people around them back it?
factors.detail: Two parts, both required. Can they say yes today without anyone else's approval, and will the people close to them — partner, spouse, business partner — support the decision rather than talk them out of it afterwards. Speaking in the first person throughout with no mention of anyone else is a strong signal; so is explicitly saying a partner is on board.

bands.text: Someone else decides, or a partner was named as an obstacle rather than a supporter.
Probably able to decide but a second party exists and was never resolved either way.
Sole decision-maker, or the people around them were named and confirmed as supportive.

factors.name: Financial Capacity
factors.question: Can the prospect actually pay what this offer costs?
factors.detail: Capacity, not willingness — willingness belongs to the beliefs above. Look for what they said about income, savings, existing spend on similar things, or what they have already invested in trying to solve this. Having previously paid for a comparable programme is the strongest single signal. Treat "I'd have to find it" as low. If money never came up on the call at all, return 0 rather than a middle score.

bands.text: Stated or clearly implied inability to pay at this level, or the price would be a genuine hardship.
Mixed or indirect signals. They implied they could find it, or spend on something adjacent, without confirming capacity at this level.
Demonstrated capacity — current income, prior spend on something comparable, or funds explicitly available.

factors.name: ICP Fit
factors.question: Is this the kind of buyer the offer is actually built for?
factors.detail: Judge against the offer context at the top of this prompt: the situation, stage, niche and starting point the offer is designed for. This is the one factor that is about fit rather than state of mind, and it is the one marketing controls most directly. A perfect-fit prospect with no urgency is a nurture problem; a poor-fit prospect with high urgency is a targeting problem.

bands.text: Wrong buyer. Outside the niche, at the wrong stage, or wanting something the offer does not do.
Adjacent. Recognisably in the market but off the described profile in stage, niche or starting point.
Squarely the intended buyer, matching the offer context on situation, stage and goal.

patterns: High Solution Belief with mid Self-Efficacy is the most closeable pattern there is: they believe the method works and know they cannot do it alone. Lead with proof and structure — people like them who got the result.
High Solution Belief with low Self-Efficacy is coachable but fragile. They will buy the idea and stall on themselves. It needs an identity reframe before the price, not a payment plan after it.
Low Solution Belief with high Self-Efficacy is the hardest pattern. They think they can do it alone and doubt the method. Nothing closes until doubt is built first.
High everything with low Urgency is a real buyer on the wrong day. The mistake is discounting; the fix is a forcing function or a scheduled return.
High Pain with low Financial Capacity is the most expensive lead to chase. It feels closeable on the call and does not pay.

objections.intro: Record which objections were actually voiced, so the pattern across calls is visible. An objection counts when the prospect raised it, whether or not the caller resolved it. If the call ended before any objection surfaced, answer with None raised and leave the primary objection null.

types.name: Price
types.detail: The number itself is the problem — too expensive, cannot afford it, needs it cheaper.

types.name: Timing
types.detail: Wants to start later. A better month, after something else finishes, not right now.

types.name: Partner
types.detail: Needs to speak to a spouse, business partner, or anyone else before deciding.

types.name: Think about it
types.detail: Wants to defer with no reason given. The classic stand-in for an objection they did not name.

types.name: Doubts the method
types.detail: Not convinced this approach works, or not convinced it works when this provider delivers it.

types.name: Doubts themselves
types.detail: Believes the offer works but not that they personally will follow through on it.

types.name: Tried before
types.detail: A previous course, coach or programme failed them and this looks like the same thing.

types.name: Comparing options
types.detail: Weighing a named alternative, or shopping the category before committing.

types.name: No time
types.detail: Believes it works and cannot see where the hours to do it would come from.

types.name: None raised
types.detail: No objection was voiced — including calls that ended before the offer was made.

bonusFlags.question: Did the caller give away consulting or strategy before getting a commitment?
Was a follow-up booked when a harder push was warranted?
Was the price dropped before the caller confirmed the prospect was certain about the solution?
Which of the seven beliefs was weakest or missing on this call?

narrative.heading: Best moment
narrative.instruction: The single strongest move the caller made. Quote it.

narrative.heading: Biggest miss
narrative.instruction: The single highest-leverage thing that could have been different. Quote it.

narrative.heading: The moment
narrative.instruction: Identify the single highest-leverage point on the call where a different move would have changed the outcome. Quote the transcript with its [mm:ss], explain what happened, what should have happened, and why it matters. Two to four sentences.

narrative.heading: Next call drill
narrative.instruction: One specific, concrete behaviour the caller can apply on their very next call. Not "work on your discovery" but "when the prospect gives a surface-level answer, say 'tell me more about that' and then wait." One or two sentences.

narrative.heading: Reading this lead
narrative.instruction: What the lead-quality factors mean for how this prospect should be handled — written about the prospect, not the caller. Name the pattern the factors form, say what it implies for the next conversation with them, and give the one move that fits it. Two to four sentences. Where one of the listed patterns applies, use it; where none does, describe what you actually see.

commercial.outcomeGuide: Customer = said yes. BAMFAM = follow-up scheduled. No offer made = unqualified or no offer given. No deal = offered but declined. No show = did not attend. REFUND = cancelled after buying.

offerMatch.heading: Was this call about the offer above?
why: A closer who sells more than one product books all of it into one calendar, because the calendar belongs to the closer and not to the product. So a call can be recorded correctly, scored correctly, and still be none of this client's business.

Nothing else on the row can tell the difference. The closer, the price, the outcome and the length all look identical either way. Until this field existed the only defence was a hand-written list of names, which held whatever somebody remembered to add to it.

One such call reached this tracker in August 2026: an Amazon FBA mentorship sold for $4,000 by a closer who also sells the client's trading offer. The transcript said so plainly in the first two minutes — the caller introduced himself as part of a different team, and named a different product. It cost three days and two wrong rulings to work out by hand what the transcript said outright.
instruction: Decide whether the thing being SOLD on this call is the offer described under 'The offer being sold' above. Judge the product, not the prospect: someone who runs an e-commerce shop can still be buying a trading mentorship, and that is 'this offer'.

Quote the line that decides it, with its [mm:ss]. Strongest evidence first: the caller naming the product or the team they work for, then the structure and price of what was pitched, then what the prospect says they came for.

Answer 'different offer' ONLY when the transcript positively identifies a different product — a different name, a different team, a different thing being delivered. A call that is simply hard to follow is 'unclear'.

Answer 'unclear' whenever you cannot tell. That is a real answer and it costs nothing: an unclear call is still counted, it is only flagged for a person to read. A wrong 'different offer' deletes a real sale from the client's revenue, so the burden of proof sits on that verdict alone.
